title: ר' נחוניא בן הקנה

paragraphs:
R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah, Avot 3; Mishnah Berakhot 4:2. In Temple times, R. Yoḥanan ben Zakkai's student, a great and pious sage. He composed Sefer HaBahir on Kabbalah's mysteries. He appears to be R. Neḥunya the Great, whom R. Akiva asked by what merit he had lived long. He answered that he accepted no gifts, did not insist on his rights, and was generous with money—the last is absent in Heilprin’s Ein Yaakov [the Daat digital text includes it]—Benei HaIr 28a. But there it later says—should read earlier—that they asked R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah about longevity, and he answered that he had not gained honor through his colleague's disgrace, nor had his colleague's curse gone up with him [to bed], and he was generous with money. These two traits belonged to R. Neḥunya the Great. Perhaps refusing gifts meant not gaining honor through a colleague's disgrace, when gifts were given to him and not to his colleague. Mishnah Berakhot 4 says he prayed on entering the study house.

R. Yoḥanan ben Zakkai said, 'R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah's words appear correct,' Bava Batra 10b. Calling him R. Neḥunya suggests he was not his student. He was teacher of R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest (see his entry), and of R. Yishmael, R. Akiva's colleague. Yishmael received Kabbalah's mysteries from him; he brought him down to the chariot to learn whether Heaven decreed the ten royal martyrs' fate; see there at length. The introduction to מג״ע [provisionally Megalleh Amukot] says R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah composed Sefer HaPeli'ah: Neḥunya, including one for the whole word, has Peli'ah's numerical value. In Eduyot and Ḥullin 129b he disagrees with R. Eliezer and R. Yehoshua (see below, R. Neḥunya ben Elḥanan); 'ben Elkanah' appears a scribal error, rather it is simply R. Neḥunya.

Yuḥasin writes [in Seder HaDorot], concerning R. Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest above: 'It is known R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah did not see the destruction.' This knowledge escaped me: how does he know? On the contrary, he raised R. Yishmael ben Elisha to the chariot to learn whether Heaven decreed the ten martyrs' fate. R. Yishmael was the first of the ten, with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel the elder, at the destruction. Yuḥasin holds they were killed after it; thus R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah saw the destruction.

I found an exceedingly old handwritten Kabbalah book and thought to copy it here, since I do not know its generation. As he descends from R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah, I placed it here. It says: Kanah [son of] Even Gedud, whose son was Naḥum, of R. Neḥunya ben HaKanah's exalted family, who understood Torah's secrets [the opening genealogy's syntax requires review], said: In the year 4000 my father dreamed, 'Your daughter-in-law, your son's wife, is pregnant and will bear you a son; call him Naḥum.' My wife then bore a male and I named him Naḥum. At three he recognized his Creator and began speaking for three consecutive days on 'I am the Lord your God.' My late father recoiled before him. Three men arrived with a small boy among them: one black, signifying might, the attribute of judgment, etc.; the second white, signifying lovingkindness, etc.; the third green, signifying Tiferet; the boy signified Malkhut, etc. My blood fled when I saw them, but Naḥum strengthened himself, approached, seized their garments' corners and asked why they had come, etc. My father took the boy, realizing he had begun asking what is above and below, etc. He told me, 'Kanah, take your son Naḥum, have them sit before you, and write for yourselves the positive and negative commandments and their root,' etc. The men who had come to my father still stood there. Naḥum asked why they had come. The white one answered, 'To teach you Scripture,' etc. For ten years we sat before my father and learned wondrous things; after thirteen years my father died, etc. He said to the three men, to his father Kanah and his grandfather Even Gedud, 'Why,' etc. End of quotation.
